title: Chapter 89 – Fruit
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The door opens on a stair full of people.

Jian had expected the monk. He had expected, at worst, Bai. He did not expect forty disciples packed shoulder to shoulder up the spiral, in gray and white and the dark green of the Library, every face turned down toward the iron door with the same stunned, hungry look. Above them, at the turn of the stair, stand three Elders in plum-colored robes.

The monk stands in front of him with his arms spread, like a man holding back a river.

"The chamber is under the protection of the Pill Hall," he says, in a voice that carries up the stair. "No one passes."

Nobody speaks. In the silence Jian can hear the Library overhead, a low murmur of hundreds of people trying not to breathe loudly. He can feel them, too. His new Qi sense reaches out like a hand opening in the dark, and it brings back forty small bright flames, some steady, some flickering, and above them, at the turn of the stair, three that burn like furnaces.

One of the three is Qin Hao.

He is a tall, spare man with a gray-streaked beard and a face like a closed door. He has not moved since the door opened. His eyes rest on Jian with no expression at all.

Then a heavy step comes down the stair behind him, and a rumpled voice says, "Make way. Make way, I said. Is no one in this Sect capable of standing aside for a man carrying plums?"

Bai pushes through the crowd with a paper twist in one hand and his robe on crooked. He reaches the monk and stops. He looks at Jian, at the gray face and the bitten lip and the tunic stiff with dried sweat. For the length of a breath, something moves behind the pale eyes. It is gone before anyone could name it.

"Well," says Bai. "It worked."

"Elder," says Qin Hao, from the stair. "What worked?"

"The experiment." Bai eats a plum. "You will recall, Elder Qin, that I was granted leave last spring to test the Founders' formula on a volunteer from the Pill Hall. A modest trial, a low-grade pill, a single apprentice of good root and bad luck." He swallows. "I did not expect the sky to notice. I apologize to the Court for the disturbance."

The silence on the stair changes. It is not relief. It is the sound of forty people deciding whether to believe an old man's lie.

"A low-grade pill," says Qin Hao.

"Very low."

"Did not produce that." The Elder's gaze does not leave Jian. "That was a Qi tide, Elder Bai. It reached the Mountain Gate."

"It was a very good apprentice."

A long pause.

"We will speak of this in the hall," says Qin Hao. "Tonight. All of us." He turns, and his plum robe swings, and the stair empties as quickly as a drained basin, disciples melting away up the spiral without a word. Only the monk remains, and Bai, and Jian, and the sound of a dozen retreating footsteps.

When the last has gone, Bai lets out a very long breath and sags against the wall.

"Four days," he says.

"Elder?"

"I need four days. Perhaps five." He rubs his face. "I told them it was an experiment, which is a lie, and a poor one, and they will know it. But a poor lie is still a wall. They cannot question you while the Pill Hall holds you under study. The Founders' Rule is on my side for once." The pale eyes are bloodshot. "You will go back into that room, and you will stay there, and you will do whatever it is that you do with your face when you are thinking. And on the fifth day I shall walk you out, in front of everyone, and say you are well."

"And the Elders' meeting?"

"I shall attend it." A thin smile. "I have been to a great many. I know where the chairs are."

Jian bows.

It is a small, stiff bow, the bow of a boy who can barely stand. Bai waves a hand at it, irritable, then lays the same hand briefly on Jian's shoulder. It is warm and heavy. It trembles very slightly.

"Eat something first," says the old man.

* * *

That night Bai comes down the stair alone, and he does not look like a man who has won.

He sits on the stone floor of the chamber with his back to the iron door and his robe in a heap around him, and for some time he says nothing. He has brought a flask. He pours two cups, pushes one across the floor, and drinks the other.

"Four hours," he says. "They kept me four hours."

"Who spoke?"

"Everyone. Elder Mu of the Law Hall wished to know why a Pill Hall experiment had produced a Qi tide that moved the weathervane on the Mountain Gate. Elder Zhou of the Treasury wished to know what it cost. Elder Qin did not wish to know anything. He sat with his hands folded and watched me lie." The pale eyes crease without humor. "He is very good at it. I have watched him do it to better liars than I."

"Did they believe you?"

"No. But they could not disprove it, and in this Sect that is nearly the same." Bai turns the empty cup in his fingers. "Under the Founders' Rule, a subject of study may not be questioned without the Pill Hall's leave for the length of the study. I wrote the study this afternoon. It is nine days long. I backdated it to the fourth of last month."

Jian stares at him. "That is forgery."

"That is paperwork." A pause. "I have been Alchemist to this Sect for ninety years, boy. I have signed ten thousand documents and read perhaps a hundred. Nobody checks the dates."

"And Qin Hao?"

"Qin Hao asked a single question at the end." The old man sets down the cup. "He asked whether the Founders' pill in my furnace room was still sealed. I told him it was. He said, Good. Then he asked who held the key." His voice drops. "I said I did. He thanked me, very civilly, and went away."

The chamber is quiet. The muffling array glows faintly overhead, a few of its outer marks gone dark.

"He knows," says Jian.

"He suspects. It is not the same, and the difference is the only thing I have left." Bai gets to his feet with a grunt. "Nine days. Use them. I cannot buy you a tenth."

At the door he stops without turning.

"When you came to my furnace, you were a boy with a hot hand and a very bad lie," he says. "I thought you would be useful. I did not think I would grow fond of you. It is most inconvenient." The iron groans. "Eat the rice."

* * *

The Seal heals slowly, and the Fruit comes with it.

He has not been looking for it. He has been lying in the chamber for a day and a night, drinking water, forcing down rice, letting the new Qi settle in the channels like silt in a pond. The panel has been quiet. The Seal under his breastbone has been a dull bruise that throbs with every breath. He has been thinking about nothing at all.

On the second morning of the extension, the Canon speaks.

It is not a voice. It never is. It is the Seed Canon's own shape, the scrolls he has recited every night since the Wellmaster's cellar, rising in his mind like a tide coming in over flat sand. The first part, the Seed, he has known for months: the slow breath, the root that drinks, the green thing waking in the dark. The second, the Sprout, he learned in the mine. He has sensed the third, the Bloom, and half walked its path.

The fourth part has been waiting.

Fruit.

He had read it once in Heng's copy and not understood it. It is the shortest section, only forty characters, and its first line says only: When the base is laid, the tree bears.

He sits cross-legged, with his back against the wall and his palms open on his knees. He lets his breath fall slow. He turns his attention inward, to the new six-sided base in his dantian, pale gold, spinning in its measured way, and the nine bright channels that run out from it like the ribs of a leaf. He reaches for the Canon's forty characters.

The base turns.

It turns once, twice, and on the third turn a thread of pale green Qi uncurls from its edge and slides into the nearest channel, the one along the inside of his left arm. It is a small thread, no thicker than a hair. It moves up the arm to the elbow, over the shoulder, across the collarbone. It reaches the heart.

And it stops, as if it had come to a gate.

He holds very still.

The Canon's forty characters repeat, soft and steady, in the back of his mind. The thread of green does not move. It quivers, and a very thin pressure begins to build in the arm, a feeling of something being asked, not forced.

Give way, the Canon seems to say. Give way and be remade.

He knows, with a clear cold certainty, that this is the cost. The Fruit does not come free. It asks a channel, one channel, to be remade into something else, and the old shape will be lost. He cannot undo it. He cannot take it back. If he lets the thread pass, the vein along his left arm will change forever.

One vein. He thinks of the nine bright channels. One of nine. For what?

The Canon does not tell him. It never tells. It lets him think of the Garden, of the first green shoot in the cold, and of what a seed does when it is old enough to bear.

He lets the thread pass.

* * *

It is not pain, quite. It is more like being unwoven.

The vein along his arm goes white first. Then it goes cold, then hot, then a color he has no name for, and for a minute that feels like an hour, his left arm is not his arm at all but a pale river of light with a boy's bones inside it. He grits his teeth. He breathes. He does not move.

Pebble, curled in the crook of his knee, whimpers.

Then the light folds in on itself, and the arm is only an arm again, thin and white, with a faint green tracery under the skin that he has never seen before. It lies across his knee like a gift from another body.

He turns it over. The tracery runs from the wrist to the elbow in a single branching line, like a sprig of fern drawn with a very fine brush. When he presses it with his thumb, it glows.

The panel brightens at the edge of his sight.

```
SEED CANON — FRUIT (first bearing).
Left-arm vein: reshaped permanently (Spring Vein).
Effect: living growth Qi may be drawn through the vein
and held; held growth Qi can be spent to mend flesh
or hasten a healing process.
Limit: one draw per day. Winter penalty: the vein
numbs below freezing. Cannot be reversed.
CE: 6 (no cost; Canon-native).
```

He reads it slowly.

Spring. It is not a Qi technique so much as a trade. The Canon has taken a channel out of the ordinary map of his body and given it a new purpose, one he can use, and one he can never put back. He flexes his hand. The tracery pulses once, faintly green, in time with his heart.

Growth Qi. He looks at the stone floor, the gray ceiling, the dry reed mat. There is nothing living in the chamber but himself and the pangolin.

He lifts a hand toward Pebble. "May I?"

Small, says Pebble. Take small.

He lays two fingers on the pangolin's back. The tracery on his wrist brightens, and a single warm drop of something travels through the vein, like honey in a straw. It is faint. It is clean. It tastes of rain on cut grass. Pebble gives a startled squeak, and then, to Jian's surprise, a long contented sigh.

Good, says Pebble. Good. Warm.

Jian sits very still.

"It will not be enough to mend a body," he says aloud. "But it will mend a bruise."

He lays his right hand over his breastbone, where the Seal still aches. The Spring Vein pulses. A green thread of Qi, no thicker than a hair, slips out of his left arm, across his chest, and down into the throbbing place beneath his ribs. The ache eases by perhaps a tenth.

He laughs.

It is a quiet, astonished laugh, and it hurts. But it is the first real laughter he has had in weeks.

* * *

* * *

He tests the limits of it on the second afternoon, because a gift he cannot measure is a debt he cannot count.

The first test is the plant. In the jade box beside the mat, wrapped in damp cloth, lies the stub of his mother's Heartroot, a thumb's length, still faintly green at the cut. He lays his palm over it and lets the Spring Vein open.

The thread of Qi flows out of the root and into his arm, thin and sweet, and it is much richer than what he drew from Pebble. He feels it at once, in the marrow of his forearm, a warm surge that sets the old bruises on his ribs humming. Then he looks down and sees what the draw has done. The cut end of the Heartroot has gone gray. A pale shrinking line is crawling up it, like frost over a window, and the green of the skin dulls to the color of old wax.

He takes his hand away.

The root does not recover. It lies in its cloth, a husk, dry and light, with no more life in it than a twig. He sets it down very gently, as one sets down a thing one has broken.

Nine years, he thinks. My mother kept it nine years.

The panel gives a small flat chime.

```
NOTE: Spring Vein draws from the living source.
Source consumed: Heartroot (stub). Not reversible.
Reminder: draw only from sources you can spare.
```

He does not answer it. He sits with the dead root in his lap and the taste of rain on his tongue, and the green tracery on his arm pulses once, in time with his heart, as if asking a question.

Every advantage has a price, he thinks. I knew that. I did not think it would be so small, or so quick.

The second test is the cold.

He pours the last of the ice from the stone jug into the cup, takes it in his left hand, and holds it. The numbness comes quickly: the fingers first, then the wrist, then the whole length of the vein. The tracery dims to a faint thread. When he tries to open it, nothing happens. It is like reaching for a door in the dark and finding a wall.

He sets the cup down and flexes his stiff fingers until the feeling returns.

Winter penalty. He had read it and not understood. Now he does. A vein that drinks from the living is a vein that sleeps when the world is dead. In the snow of the Court's high terraces, on a night of hard frost, the Spring Vein will be as useless as a cut rope. He will have to remember it. He will have to remember it when it matters.

He writes both facts on the back of his list, under the six lines, in a hand that is nearly steady.

Source consumed. Winter: dead.

Then, because he is twenty-one, and tired, and very much alone, he writes a third line beneath them.

Worth it.

He looks at it for a long time. Then he crosses it out, and writes instead: Not yet known.

* * *

On the third day of the extension, someone knocks, and it is not the monk.

Three slow raps on the iron, evenly spaced. Jian is on his feet before he has decided to move, with his back to the wall and the green line in his arm gone dark. He has felt no approach. His Qi sense reaches out through the door and finds only a thin steady flame on the other side, banked low and perfectly controlled.

"Disciple Lin," says Qin Hao.

He does not raise his voice. The iron carries it anyway.

"I will not ask you to open. The Pill Hall holds you, and I am bound by the Rule. I wish only to say a few words, and for you to listen, and for no one else to hear." A pause. "The muffling array on this door is the finest in the Court. It was laid by the Founder's own hand. It does not leak."

Jian says nothing.

"You will know that I was the Elder who sent the third notice after the Wellmaster." The voice is dry and even. "I wrote that you had acted within the Rule. I wrote it because it was true. I wrote nothing about how you knew the vent, or why a Qi Refining boy was standing on the fortieth landing, or what the stair did when you walked it." Another pause. "I have been Elder for sixty years. I do not often write notes I cannot finish."

"Elder—"

"Do not answer. I did not come for an answer." The voice goes lower. "The fortieth landing has been sealed since before my grandfather was born. There is a saying, in the old registers: the Gate opens for the one it was made for. I thought it a fable. I thought so until I felt the tide this week."

Jian's mouth is dry.

"I will not stop you," says Qin Hao. "I want you to know that. I am the last man in this Court who would. But there are others who would, and some of them are not on the Council, and I do not know all their names." The flame beyond the door shifts, and Jian hears the faint creak of a man rising to his feet. "When you come out, do not come out alone. That is all."

Footsteps. The long slow tread of an old man going up a stair. Then silence.

Jian stands with his shoulders against the stone and his heart going hard.

Not on the Council, he thinks. Not on the Council.

He thinks of the hooded stranger who raised an open palm. He thinks of the iron-brown stain on the Deacon's glass, and the knotted thread under the Reed Courtyard cot. He thinks of the Master, dead in the array with his Wells beyond Wells, and what the Master had said about the order.

The Master was never the whole of it.

Pebble pushes its nose into his hand.

Once the tide of the day has gone out of him, he sits in the dark and tallies what he has.

A base. A vein. A pangolin, a dead root, a pill of gray pewter in a box of jade. Six points of energy that will not climb for days. A Seal that aches like a broken rib. An old man upstairs who has forged a document for him, and an older one on the stair who has promised not to stop him. He sets them in a row in his mind, as he once set the reagents on the table, and finds that the row is longer than it was a month ago.

It is also thinner. Every item on it is a debt.

He does not mind. A debt, his father used to say, is only a promise that someone else believes in you. He has never been believed in by so many people at once. It is heavy, and it is warm, and he finds, somewhat to his surprise, that he would not put it down.

* * *

On the fourth day of the extension, he runs the season-cycle.

It is the last line of the Fruit: Run the four seasons, and the tree is known. He has never understood it. He thinks he does now. The Canon is a wheel, and a wheel has a rim. The Seed is spring, the Sprout is summer, the Bloom is autumn, and the Fruit is the turn of winter into spring. A cultivator who runs the wheel once, with a base beneath him, completes a cycle.

He closes his eyes and begins.

The Qi flows down the Spring Vein, and the world around him changes. He is in a green place, a field after rain. The Qi turns warm: summer, the heavy bright heat of noon, the hum of insects. It turns gold and slow: autumn, the full ripe weight of harvest. It turns cold and clear: the frost, the stillness, the dark under the snow.

And then it should turn again. It should loop back to green. It does not.

At the edge of winter, where the wheel should close, the Qi hits a wall.

It is a smooth gray wall, without a seam. Beyond it, he can feel, something waits. A fifth season. A part that is not in Heng's copy, not in the Founder's notes, not in any scroll he has seen. The Qi presses against the wall and the wall presses back, and the Seal under his sternum, sore and bruised, gives a single deep note that goes through him like a struck bell.

He opens his eyes.

The chamber is dark. The lamp has burned out. In the black he can see only the tracery on his left arm, faintly green, and the wall of his own breath, rising and falling.

The Canon is not finished.

He knows it as plainly as he has ever known anything. The Seed Canon, the thing he has built his life on for four years, is a lock with a key missing. It ends at the point where it should begin again. It was cut off. Or hidden.

Part Two.

He turns the words over in his mind. They taste of cold iron.

The Seal hums. It is a very soft sound, almost too low to hear, and it comes not from his own chest but from somewhere far above him: from the stair, the Library, the courts, the mountain. A thread of sound runs up out of the chamber and into the dark, up past the Library and the Court and the Mountain Gate to a landing forty steps above, where a door of old black stone stands sealed under a row of cracked marks.

He does not need the panel to tell him. He follows the sound in his head, step by step, and at the end of it, with perfect certainty, he knows where the second half of the Canon is kept.

Behind the lock.

His left arm glows.

Pebble lifts its head. Door? it asks.

"Yes," says Jian.

Open?

"Soon."

He lies back on the cold stone, with the tracery pulsing under his sleeve and the dull ache in his chest, and for the first time since the cradle he does not feel like a boy who is being led. He feels like one who is walking.

Above him, the Library bell begins to toll the evening. Somewhere in the Court, an old man is putting on his best robe and going to lie to the Elders. And in the dark, the Sect waits for what Lin Jian will do next.
